rows: Workers must have access to suitable toilets and handwashing facilities.
Workers need suitable clothing storage and changing facilities where special clothing is used.
A place to rest and eat meals should be provided.
Workplaces should have fresh air and a reasonable working temperature.
Lighting should be suitable for the work.
Workrooms need enough space and suitable workstations and seating.
Premises, floors and traffic routes should be maintained and kept clear.
A facility list or floor plan does not prove that welfare provision is adequate on every shift.
Conclusions require capacity, cleanliness, accessibility, staffing, disability needs, maintenance and actual availability evidence.
Lighting should be suitable for the task and workplace.
Lighting design should avoid glare, deep shadows and confusing reflections.
Emergency lighting should support safe escape where normal lighting can fail.
Workers need enough space to move and access workstations safely.
Work equipment and documents should be stored without obstructing movement.
Cramped workspaces can affect safety and human performance.
Room volume guidance is a minimum and may be insufficient for some layouts or tasks.
Lighting and space should be reviewed when workstations or processes change.
A lux value or room volume alone does not prove suitable working conditions.
Conclusions require task visual demand, contrast, glare, emergency lighting, layout, occupancy and movement evidence.
MEWPs should be selected to suit the task, height, reach and site conditions.
Operators must be trained and competent.
Ground conditions and supporting surfaces should be checked.
Overhead structures and power lines must be considered.
Crushing and trapping risks require suitable planning and controls.
Platforms should not be overloaded beyond their rated capacity.
Fall protection should follow the machine type, task and risk assessment.
Inspection, maintenance and pre-use checks should be completed.
An operator card or machine inspection does not prove a particular lift is safe.
Use conclusions require machine type, ground, reach, load, wind, overhead hazards, rescue and supervision evidence.
Work that may disturb underground services should be planned before excavation starts.
Plans and service records should be obtained and interpreted carefully.
Service-locating equipment should be used by trained people.
Trial holes and safe digging practices help confirm service positions.
All services should be treated as live until proved otherwise.
Mechanical excavation should be controlled near suspected services.
Service owners should be consulted where information is uncertain.
Emergency arrangements should address strikes, leaks, fire and electric shock.
A utility plan or locator signal does not prove exact depth and position.
Conclusions require current records, scanning, markings, trial holes, excavation method, service status and supervision evidence.
